drills.title: Create, fill and query a table
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a JDBC program that builds a throw-away in-memory database, adds three orders and prints the units per product, A-Z. Two lines do not belong.
lines: st.execute("CREATE TABLE sales (product TEXT, qty INTEGER)");
String sql = "SELECT product, SUM(qty) FROM sales GROUP BY product ORDER BY product";
drills.explain: The Connection and the Statement are opened in try-with-resources, so they are closed even when an error happens. A query returns a ResultSet that starts before the first row: while (rs.next()) moves forward and is false at the end (there is no hasNext). JDBC columns are numbered from 1, so the first column is getString(1), and getString(0) would throw.

drills.title: A query with a ? placeholder
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the region travels as a parameter and the program prints the total for West.
code: public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
st.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (region TEXT, amount INTEGER)");
String sql = "SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE region = ___";
drills.explain: A ? marks where a value goes; the value is sent separately with setString, so it can never change the meaning of the SQL (no injection). In quotes ('?') it would be plain text and there would be no parameter at all. Placeholder numbers start at 1, not 0. A ResultSet starts before its first row, so rs.next() must run before getInt: first() is not allowed on SQLite's forward-only cursor and hasNext does not exist.

drills.title: A failed credit and a rollback
drills.prompt: Move Rs. 500 from account 1 to account 9, which does not exist. Type exactly what the program prints, one line per line of output.
code: st.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER)");
System.out.println(st.executeUpdate("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1"));
System.out.println(st.executeUpdate("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 9"));
try (ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1")) {
drills.explain: executeUpdate returns how many rows it changed: 1 for the debit, and 0 for the credit because there is no account 9 (SQL raises no error for that, you have to look at the count). With auto-commit off, both updates are still pending, so rollback() undoes the debit as well and the balance is back to 1000. All or nothing is what a transaction gives you.

drills.title: The discount that vanished
drills.prompt: A Lamp (2 x Rs. 800, 15% off) and a Tea (Rs. 120) should give a revenue of 1480.0, but the program prints a different number. Click the faulty line, then choose the fix.
code: public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
st.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (qty INTEGER, price INTEGER, discount_pct INTEGER)");
String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - discount_pct / 100)) FROM orders";
fixed_code: public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
st.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (qty INTEGER, price INTEGER, discount_pct INTEGER)");
String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - discount_pct / 100.0)) FROM orders";
options: String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - discount_pct / 100.0)) FROM orders";
String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - CAST(discount_pct / 100 AS REAL))) FROM orders";
String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - discount_pct / 100) * 1.0) FROM orders";
String sql = "SELECT SUM(qty * price * (1 - discount_pct) / 100) FROM orders";
drills.explain: In SQL, as in Java, a whole number divided by a whole number is a whole number: 15 / 100 is 0, so the discount disappears and the Lamp costs the full 1600. Make one side a decimal (100.0). Casting after the division, or multiplying by 1.0 at the end, is too late because the 0 is already there, and (1 - discount_pct) / 100 is a different formula.

drills.title: Review the AI's order counter
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this JDBC helper. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are two).
code: static int countOrders(Connection conn, String region) throws SQLException {
ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE region = '" + region + "'");
public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
st.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (region TEXT, amount INTEGER)");

issues.text: The region is glued into the SQL text with +
issues.why: A region such as West' OR '1'='1 changes the meaning of the query and returns every row (SQL injection). Use a PreparedStatement with WHERE region = ? and ps.setString(1, region).

issues.text: The Statement and the ResultSet are never closed
issues.why: Every call leaves both open until the connection closes, and on a file database it can keep the file locked. Put them in try-with-resources so they are closed even when an error happens.

non_issues.why: JDBC columns are numbered from 1, so getInt(1) reads the first column. getInt(0) would throw.

non_issues.text: main must call conn.commit() after the INSERT
non_issues.why: A new JDBC connection is in auto-commit mode: every statement is saved at once. commit() is only needed after setAutoCommit(false).

non_issues.text: jdbc:sqlite::memory: loses the tables between the two countOrders calls
non_issues.why: An in-memory database lives as long as its connection, and both calls use the same conn.

non_issues.text: COUNT(*) returns a long, so getInt cannot be used
non_issues.why: getInt converts the value, and a small count fits easily. Use getLong only when the number could pass about 2 billion.

drills.explain: In generated database code look at how the SQL is built and who closes what. Both problems also hide in code that works perfectly in a demo.
